outputText: Run onesource to create a file with a directory tree followed by the contents of each selected file. Clear file paths give AI the project background it needs to discuss issues and changes.
outputTree: Directory tree: keep the relationships between files and folders.
outputFiles: File blocks: identify the source of every code section by path.
outputTokens: Token estimate: understand the approximate context size before sharing.
selectText: Use include to select file types and exclude to omit unwanted paths. Exclusions take priority; the directory tree can also have its own filtering rules.
previewText: A dry run lists selected files and estimates tokens for the full output without creating a file. When ready, you can also copy the context directly to your clipboard.
reuseText: Save named profiles for different tasks. Settings resolve in this order: command-line options → selected profile → built-in defaults.
notesTitle: Predictable, with answers when you need them.
defaultsText: Defaults skip files larger than 500 KiB and common paths such as .env, private keys, node_modules, and target. Size and binary checks decide whether content is attached, but do not remove paths from the directory tree.
explainTitle: Find out why a file is missing
explainText: The explain command reports content and tree decisions separately, including ignore rules, filters, size, and binary checks. Pass an actual file path to inspect its result.
reviewText: Default filters help skip common sensitive paths. Still check the output for secrets and content that should not be shared. File blocks are framing for AI readability, not a security boundary.
title: OneSource — Package Your Codebase for AI
description: Turn your codebase into reusable AI context in one command. OneSource organizes your directory tree and file contents locally.
tagline: Turn your codebase into AI context in one command.
intro: OneSource is a local command-line tool that packages your codebase into a single .onesource file. A directory tree and selected file contents form clear, reusable AI context, with an estimated token count.
estimate: Token counts are estimates. Actual usage varies by model and tokenizer.
structureText: A filtered directory tree and clearly framed file blocks give AI both project structure and code. Set independent filtering rules for the tree when needed.
localText: Organize files locally. Default filters respect rules such as .gitignore and skip common sensitive, generated, and dependency paths. Review the output before sharing.
profileText: Save recurring scan settings in .onesourcerc and reuse them with named profiles. Override settings with command-line options whenever you need to.
socialAlt: OneSource — package your codebase into reusable AI context
installTitle: Install OneSource. Give AI your project context.
cargoText: With Rust installed, install the free, MIT-licensed OneSource CLI using Cargo.
unixText: The installer downloads the latest release to /usr/local/bin and may request sudo permission.
windowsText: Run the installer in PowerShell, then restart your terminal to refresh PATH.
quickText: Run these commands from your project directory. Preview the selected files first, then create a .onesource file or copy the context to your clipboard. Review the output before sharing it with AI.
downloadText: Download portable binaries from GitHub Releases
quickNote: Packaging runs locally; it does not upload your code. Token counts are estimates.
guideDescription: Install OneSource on Windows, macOS or Linux. Verify your installation, create your first AI context, update the CLI and troubleshoot common issues.
guideIntro: Choose your platform below. Install the CLI, check that it works, then package a project into reusable AI context. No Rust installation is required when using a prebuilt binary.
guideCopyFailed: Copy unavailable. Select the command and copy it manually.
guideWindowsIntro: Open PowerShell from the Start menu. The prebuilt Windows executable targets x86_64. Run the following command with an internet connection.
guideWindowsAfter: The installer downloads the latest GitHub release into %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\onesource and adds that folder to your user PATH. Close and reopen your terminal, then follow “Verify installation” below.
guideMacosIntro: Open Terminal. With curl and an internet connection available, run the command below. The installer selects the Intel or Apple Silicon binary automatically.
guideUnixAfter: The installer places onesource in /usr/local/bin. It may ask for your sudo password to move the executable into that folder. Next, verify the installation below.
guideLinuxIntro: Open a terminal with Bash and curl available. The released Linux binary targets x86_64 with GNU libc. For other architectures, use Cargo to build for your machine instead of running the network installer.
guideCargoIntro: If Rust and Cargo are installed, build and install OneSource for your machine. A working native linker and the build prerequisites for your platform are also required.
guideCargoAfter: Cargo normally installs commands in ~/.cargo/bin (Windows: %USERPROFILE%\.cargo\bin). With a custom CARGO_HOME, use its bin folder instead. Make sure that folder is on PATH; reopen the terminal after installing Rust.
guidePortableIntro: Open GitHub Releases and download the asset matching your platform. These are executables, not archives. On macOS or Linux, rename the downloaded file to onesource; on Windows, keep onesource.exe.
guidePortableAfter: In the folder containing the downloaded executable, run the matching commands below. Portable executables do not modify PATH; use ./onesource or .\onesource.exe for subsequent commands, or add their folder to PATH yourself.
guideVerifyIntro: In a new terminal, check the installed version and available commands. A version beginning with “onesource” and the help text confirm that the executable is available. The version number depends on the release you installed.
guideFirstIntro: Replace my-project with your project folder. Preview the selected files and token estimate, then create the output file.
guideFirstAfter: OneSource creates <project-name>.onesource in the current working directory, containing a directory tree and selected file contents. To copy context without creating a file, run the following command.
guideLocalNote: Packaging runs locally and does not upload your code. Review the output before sharing it with AI. Token counts are estimates.
guideUpdateIntro: For a compatible prebuilt installation, download the latest GitHub release and replace the current executable with the built-in update command. On Windows, replacement finishes after the process exits; verify in a new terminal.
guideCargoUpdate: For Cargo installations, especially on architectures without a matching release asset, rebuild using Cargo. This preserves the native build for your platform.
guidePermissionUpdate: If updating fails because the installation folder is not writable, rerun the original installer or replace a portable executable in a folder you can write to.
guideFaqPathText: Reopen the terminal first. Check that the installation folder listed above is on PATH. In PowerShell, use Get-Command onesource; on macOS/Linux, use command -v onesource. A portable executable needs its relative or absolute path. If multiple installations exist, these commands show which one is being used.
guideFaqPermissionText: For a manually downloaded macOS/Linux executable, run chmod +x onesource in its folder. Installing into /usr/local/bin may require sudo. If you cannot write to the system folder, keep a portable executable in a folder you own.
guideFaqDownloadText: Check access to GitHub and your network connection. GitHub API requests may be rate limited; retry later or download the matching asset directly from Releases.
guideFaqArchText: Check the platform table and download the matching executable. On macOS/Linux, uname -m shows the machine architecture. For platforms without a matching asset, build with Cargo and also update through Cargo.
guideFaqClipboardText: Clipboard access may be unavailable in remote terminals or environments without a desktop session. Run onesource without --copy to save a file instead.
guidePathText: Windows installer uses %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\onesource and updates User PATH; restart your terminal. Unix installer moves to /usr/local/bin, requesting sudo if needed. Cargo uses ~/.cargo/bin. For manual installs, add the containing directory to PATH; Unix users can place the binary in ~/.local/bin and add export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" to the shell startup file. On Windows add the folder in Environment Variables → User Path, then open a new terminal. Run command -v onesource or Get-Command onesource to verify which binary is selected.
guidePrepareText: Choose one installation method below. For the network installers you need access to GitHub and its API; macOS/Linux also need Bash and curl, Windows needs PowerShell. Prebuilt assets cover Windows x86_64, Linux x86_64 GNU, and macOS Intel/Apple Silicon. Other platforms should use Cargo with Rust and a native linker. After installing, verify both the command path and version before bundling a project.
guideCargoCheck: First run cargo --version. A cargo version line confirms the tool is available; if the command is missing, install Rust using the link above and open a new terminal. Only then run cargo install onesource and wait for installation to finish.
guideVerifyAfter: Expect a version line beginning with onesource and a help screen showing Usage and Options. On macOS/Linux, command -v onesource should point to the install location; on Windows use Get-Command onesource. If a different location is selected, fix PATH or run the intended executable by its full path. These checks identify a working CLI; the following preview checks actual bundling.
guidePortableSteps: Choose your OS and architecture in the table, download that named asset (not the source archive), and put it in a folder you can write to. On macOS/Linux, use uname -m to distinguish x86_64 from arm64/aarch64; then rename as described below. Running the relative path verifies the download before you decide whether to add it to PATH.
